name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,369

clue.text: Party cheers rabid, vacuous old fool

indicators.note: A vacuous thing is empty in the middle, so the word beside it keeps only the letters at its two edges.

blocks.note: a do is a party — the office do, a birthday do
ta is the British thank-you, and cheers does the same job
emptied out, rabid keeps its first and last letters only

explanation.surface: A party raises a cheer for someone raving and empty-headed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' looks political in a sentence about slogans and cheering, and is the social kind. The definition points at dotage, the feeble-mindedness that comes with great age.
explanation.definitionFit: A dotard is someone whose wits have gone with age, so old fool names both halves of it at once.

clue.text: Spotted orchard’s last fruit

definitions.note: Dapple is an adjective as well as a verb — a dapple-grey horse — so 'spotted' is describing markings here, not reporting that somebody noticed something.

indicators.note: The last of a word is the letter it ends on, and that single letter is all that is taken.

blocks.note: the letter orchard finishes on
the fruit an orchard is likeliest to be growing

explanation.surface: Someone points out the last fruit still hanging in the orchard.
explanation.walkthrough: Reading 'spotted' as the past tense of noticing is the trap; it is an adjective about markings. The rest runs on as one unbroken phrase, so nothing shows where the definition stops.
explanation.definitionFit: A dapple coat is one covered in patches of contrasting colour, which is what a spotted animal or surface looks like.

clue.text: Unthinkingly state anti-Communist slogan?

blocks.note: to produce the same tired line yet again, as a spokesman does
a Trot is a Trotskyist, so shouted as two words this tells one to clear off

explanation.surface: A slogan being chanted at a demonstration without much thought behind it.
explanation.walkthrough: Trot is British shorthand for a Trotskyist, the far-left faction Labour spent the 1980s expelling. The question mark marks the second reading as a joke rather than a dictionary sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To trot out a phrase is to produce it by reflex; split between the two words instead, it becomes an order shouted at a Trot.

clue.text: Separation initially reported in paper

indicators.note: Initially asks how words begin, so only the opening letter of each one beside it is used.

blocks.note: the first letters of the two words
the FT is the Financial Times, the pink British business daily

explanation.surface: A split between people getting its first mention in the newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reported' wants to be a signal that something is heard rather than spelt, and it is only handing over a letter. The pink paper is a stock crossword newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A rift is the gap that opens between two people who have fallen out, which is the separation the word names.

clue.text: Frozen topping that is better for keeping cold

indicators.note: Keeping a thing means holding on to it, so the letter named goes inside the word that does the keeping.

blocks.note: ie, short for the Latin id est
c is the standard abbreviation for cold, as marked on a tap
to cap a rival's offer is to better it

explanation.surface: A dessert topping that improves for being kept chilled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' has to be heard as a verb before anything moves. The definition is polar rather than culinary, which is why 'topping' reads as pudding for as long as it can.
explanation.definitionFit: An ice cap is the permanent sheet of ice lying over a polar region — frozen, and sitting on top of what it covers.

clue.text: Wins children’s game, we hear

indicators.note: What we hear is the sound of a word rather than its spelling, so the letters only have to match aloud.

blocks.note: conkers is the British playground game of swinging a horse chestnut on a string at an opponent's

explanation.surface: Someone keeps winning the children's game, going by what people say.
explanation.walkthrough: Conkers are horse chestnuts, threaded on shoelaces and smashed together in British school playgrounds every autumn. The plural s survives the crossing from sound to spelling untouched.
explanation.definitionFit: To conquer an opponent is to beat them outright, so wins covers it, and both verbs take the same third-person -s.

clue.text: Yearn for Sven, naked in bed

indicators.note: Something naked has had its covering stripped off, so the word loses the letter at each end.
In puts one thing inside another, so what comes before it is buried in the word that follows.

blocks.note: a cot is a bed
stripped of the letters at each end, Sven leaves the middle pair

explanation.surface: Sven lies undressed in bed, wanted badly by somebody.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma after 'Sven' hides that 'naked' is an instruction and not a description of him. A cot is the setter's standard three-letter bed.
explanation.definitionFit: To covet is to want badly something that is somebody else's, which is what yearning for a thing means; both verbs take an object.

clue.text: Miserable mate on crack

indicators.note: In a down entry one thing sits on top of another.

blocks.note: a pal is a mate
to have a crack at something is to have a try at it

explanation.surface: A wretched friend in a bad way on crack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' points at the drug in the surface and is the everyday 'have a crack at it'. Down clues let 'on' mean directly above, which is what fixes the order.
explanation.definitionFit: A paltry sum is a miserably small one, and the two adjectives sit in front of the same nouns — paltry wages, miserable wages.

clue.text: Present academic referee retiring

indicators.note: To retire is to go back the way you came, so the word beside it is written out in reverse.

blocks.note: a prof is an academic
a referee is a ref, turned back to front

explanation.surface: A retiring referee is handed a present by the academic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retiring' reads as the referee's final season and is a turn-round instruction. 'Present' is the verb for holding something out, not the parcel the surface pictures.
explanation.definitionFit: To proffer something is to hold it out for another to take, which is exactly what present means as a verb.

clue.text: Report of turbulent short life

indicators.note: Turbulence throws whatever it touches about, so the letters beside it will not stay in the order given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: An account of a stormy life cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Report of' at the front looks like an instruction to listen for a sound-alike, and is the definition with a link word. The letter count against the enumeration settles it.
explanation.definitionFit: The bang a gun makes is called its report, and a rifle shot is heard as precisely that single sharp crack.

clue.text: Reviewed extract from incredible Vonnegut book

indicators.note: Re-viewed is looked at a second time from the other end, so the run of letters is read backwards.
Extracting takes a run of letters already sitting in the words, in the order they stand.

blocks.note: the letters bridging 'incredibLE VONnegut', read back to front

explanation.surface: A reviewer quotes a passage out of an astonishing Vonnegut book.
explanation.walkthrough: Vonnegut wrote books, so the surface points where the definition does and the buried run is easy to walk past. Hidden answers that span a gap between words are the hardest sort to see.
explanation.definitionFit: A novel is a book-length work of fiction, so 'book' defines it by kind rather than by synonym.

clue.text: Can finally collect money

indicators.note: Finally points at the end of a word, so its closing letter is the only one used.

blocks.note: can is the American word for the lavatory, which in Britain is the loo
the letter collect ends on

explanation.surface: Somebody gets round to collecting the money at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' is doing plumbing duty rather than meaning a tin or permission. A one-word definition at the end of a short clue gives very little to aim at.
explanation.definitionFit: Loot is money carried off — from a raid, a till or a party bag — so it sits squarely inside the everyday sense of money.

clue.text: Nervous bet after tip from accountant

indicators.note: What comes after a thing is written second.
The tip of a word is its very front, so the letter it starts with is what comes away.

blocks.note: the opening letter of accountant
British for a small casual bet, the few pounds put on a horse

explanation.surface: An accountant's tip leads to a jittery wager.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip' in a sentence about accountants and betting reads as inside information, and is a letter-picking instruction. A flutter is the modest sort of bet placed at a high-street bookmaker's.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone all aflutter is fidgety and agitated, so nervous covers it — both are adjectives for the same state.

clue.text: Old man turned on generator, as observed

definitions.note: 'As observed' gives the way a thing strikes the eye rather than a one-word synonym; what is apparent is what observation shows, as opposed to what has to be worked out.

indicators.note: Something turned faces the other way, so the letters beside it are read in reverse.
In a down entry one part sits on another.

blocks.note: an old man is a pa, climbing this column
whoever generates the children is their parent

explanation.surface: The old man was seen starting the generator up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned on' reads as one phrase about switching a machine on and is two separate instructions. A generator in the wordplay is a person, not a machine.
explanation.definitionFit: What is apparent is what shows plainly on looking, so it answers to a thing taken as observed rather than inferred.

clue.text: Erect post, disguised and completely hidden from the public

indicators.note: A disguise changes how a thing looks without changing what it is, so the same letters appear in another arrangement.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Putting up a post in disguise, where nobody can see it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Erect' looks like an instruction to stand something upright, which would turn a down answer round and can do nothing in an across one. Both words are fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Top secret is the highest security classification a government gives, so what carries it is kept wholly out of public sight.

clue.text: Leaders of the Resistance are irate, talking of recent renegade

indicators.note: The leader of a word is the letter at its head, so each word in the run gives up only its first.

blocks.clueFragment: the Resistance are irate, talking of recent
blocks.note: the initial letters of those seven words, in order

explanation.surface: Angry Resistance leaders discussing somebody who has just changed sides.
explanation.walkthrough: Seven initials in a row is a long run to trust, and 'Leaders of the Resistance' reads as people rather than as an instruction. The definition is the single word at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A traitor deserts their own side and betrays it, which is what renegade names — both nouns for the same person.

clue.text: Son makes fun of baggy clothing

definitions.note: Clothing is a mass noun and the answer a plural, a swap crosswords allow because both name garments taken in bulk rather than one item.

blocks.note: s is the standard abbreviation for son, as used on a family tree
to mock somebody is to make fun of them

explanation.surface: A son teasing somebody about their loose clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: No word in the clue announces itself as an instruction, which is the mark of a plain charade. 'Makes fun of' has to be heard as a third-person verb before the letter in front of it has anywhere to go.
explanation.definitionFit: A smock is the loose overshirt worn by painters and farm workers, cut wide on purpose, which is baggy clothing.

clue.text: Cautioned Washington editor about sailors

indicators.note: Something set about a thing is wrapped round it, so the letters named last end up in the middle.

blocks.note: WA is the postal abbreviation for Washington state
the RN is the Royal Navy, Britain's sailors
ed is the standard short form of editor

explanation.surface: A Washington newspaper editor being told something about sailors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as 'on the subject of' in a sentence full of journalism and is a wrapping instruction. Washington is the state, not the capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: To warn somebody is to tell them of trouble coming, which is what cautioned reports — both past tenses of the same act.

clue.text: Shunning publicity, my head is spinning

indicators.note: A spin sends a thing round and round, so the letters beside it come to rest in a different order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: Somebody avoiding the press complains of dizziness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My head is spinning' is a complete idiom, which hides that all three of those words are fodder. 'Head' usually asks for a first letter, and here it does not.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody media shy keeps clear of interviews and cameras, which is shunning publicity.

clue.text: Grave inspiring Gray’s first elegy

indicators.note: To inspire is to breathe in, so the word draws the letter beside it inside itself.
First asks for the letter a word starts with and nothing more.

blocks.note: a grave situation is a dire one
the letter Gray starts with

explanation.surface: A grave in a churchyard that moved Gray to write his first elegy.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Gray wrote 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard', so graves, Gray and elegies belong together and no word stands out as wordplay. 'Grave' is the adjective meaning serious.
explanation.definitionFit: A dirge is the slow lament sung over the dead, and an elegy is that same mourning for the dead set down in verse.

clue.text: Story is great fun when read backwards

indicators.note: Reading backwards starts at the last letter and works towards the first.

blocks.note: something that is great fun is a gas, and that comes back the other way

explanation.surface: A tale that turns out to be hilarious if you start from the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A gas' is slang for something hugely enjoyable, and the clue leaves you to supply the article yourself. Nothing else in the sentence contributes a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A saga is a long tale of events told through from beginning to end, so story is a plain synonym.

clue.text: Nasty cases of unnerving lurgy

indicators.note: A case is what encloses a thing, so each word gives up just the letters at its two ends.

blocks.note: the outside letters of unnerving
the outside letters of lurgy — the lurgy is British slang for whatever unnamed illness is going round

explanation.surface: A nasty run of cases of some unsettling bug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cases of' fits a sentence about illness so neatly that it stops looking like an instruction. The lurgy is the joke name Britons give whatever they have caught.
explanation.definitionFit: Ugly means repellent to look at, and an ugly mood or an ugly scene is a nasty one — the same adjective either way.

clue.text: Scoundrels start to expostulate and swear

indicators.note: The start of a word is its opening letter, and only that one comes away.

blocks.note: a cur is a mongrel dog, and so a contemptible man
the opening letter of expostulate

explanation.surface: Scoundrels begin to protest loudly and turn the air blue.
explanation.walkthrough: Both ends of the clue suit the picture of a row, so the definition hides in plain sight at the back. Curs are dogs before they are people, which is where the insult gets its bite.
explanation.definitionFit: To curse is to come out with an oath, which is swear in its bad-language sense rather than its taking-an-oath one.

clue.text: Strengthen thing that teen regularly dropped

indicators.note: Letting letters go at regular intervals means losing every second one, and what stays is read in the order it stood.

blocks.note: the first letter of the run and every other one after it through 'thingthatteen'

explanation.surface: A thing the teenager keeps dropping needs making firmer.
explanation.walkthrough: Alternate-letter runs usually hide inside one or two words; this one stretches across three, so counting is the only way in. The run has to start on the very first letter to come out right.
explanation.definitionFit: To tighten a bolt, a rule or a defence is to make it firmer and harder to shift, which is strengthening it.

clue.text: Hustle involved detective

indicators.note: Something involved is tangled up, so the letters beside it are knotted into a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.surface: A detective caught up in somebody's con trick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hustle' is a con trick in the surface and a bag of six letters in the wordplay, and 'involved' means tangled rather than mixed up in a crime. Two words is the shortest a clue of this kind gets.
explanation.definitionFit: A sleuth is a detective, the word coming from the sleuth-hound that followed a trail by scent.

clue.text: Cross section of Clichy Bridge

indicators.note: A section is a piece cut out of something longer, so a run of letters is taken just as it stands.

blocks.note: the run bridging the gap in 'clicHY BRIDge'

explanation.surface: A cross-section drawing of the bridge at Clichy.
explanation.walkthrough: Clichy is a suburb on the northern edge of Paris, which is all the proper noun is there for. 'Cross' is the breeder's noun, not the adjective for annoyed.
explanation.definitionFit: A hybrid is the offspring of two different varieties, which gardeners and dog breeders call a cross.
